title: Why bread rises
examples: What part of the yeast makes the bread puff up?
Does the amount of sugar change how high the bread gets?
Why is kneading the dough so important for bread?

explain.say: Today we are learning why bread gets big and fluffy.
The living thing we use is called yeast.
Yeast needs food to survive and work. This food is sugar.
When the yeast eats the sugar, it releases a gas. This gas is carbon dioxide.
Next, we talk about kneading the dough to build gluten. Gluten gives the bread its structure.
In real life, when you bake bread, the yeast eats the sugar and releases gas. This gas gets trapped by the gluten, making the bread rise.

draw.text: Gas trapped by gluten = fluffy bread

faq.a: The gas that makes bread rise is carbon dioxide. Yeast produces this gas when it eats sugar.
asks: What gas is trapped in bread?

faq.q: Do I need sugar for bread to rise?
faq.a: While some recipes use sugar, the yeast can find food from other things in the flour. Sugar just helps the yeast work faster.
asks: Does sugar make bread rise better?

faq.a: Kneading develops gluten in the dough. Gluten is like a stretchy net that catches the gas, so the bread puffs up properly.
asks: What does kneading do to the dough?
Why do we stretch the dough?

faq.a: Gluten is a protein found in wheat flour. Kneading helps these proteins link up to form a strong, stretchy network.

faq.q: What happens if I don't knead the dough enough?
faq.a: If you do not knead enough, the gluten network will be weak. The gas will escape easily, and the bread will not rise very high.
asks: Will the bread be flat if I don't knead?
What if the dough is too soft?

facts: Yeast is a single-celled fungus, not a plant.
Yeast consumes sugars, releasing carbon dioxide gas.
Kneading develops gluten, which traps the gas.
The gas production continues until the bread bakes.

quiz.say: If the yeast is given no sugar, what will happen to the bread?

options.show: The yeast will run out of food and stop producing gas.
options.say: The yeast will run out of food and stop producing gas.

quiz.why: Yeast needs sugar to perform its chemical process of gas release.

wrong.1: This is tempting because the structure might fail, but the main issue is the lack of gas production.
wrong.2: This is tempting because yeast can sometimes produce acids, but the primary failure is physical rising.
wrong.3: This is tempting because dehydration can cause stickiness, but the problem is gas production, not moisture.

quiz.say: What is the main role of kneading dough?

options.show: To make the dough taste sweeter.
options.say: To make the dough taste sweeter.

options.show: To kill the yeast so it stops working.
options.say: To kill the yeast so it stops working.

options.show: To add more sugar to the dough.
options.say: To add more sugar to the dough.

options.show: It strengthens the gluten structure to trap the gas.
options.say: It strengthens the gluten structure to trap the gas.

quiz.why: Gluten acts like a net; kneading makes that net strong enough to hold the carbon dioxide.

wrong.0: Sugar is added separately; kneading only affects the physical structure of the dough.
wrong.1: Kneading does not kill the yeast; it simply develops the dough's physical properties.
wrong.2: Kneading is a mechanical action; it does not add ingredients like sugar.

quiz.say: If the bread is baked too quickly, what happens to the gas?

options.show: The dough shrinks back to its original size.
options.say: The dough shrinks back to its original size.

options.show: The trapped gas escapes too fast, making the bread dense.
options.say: The trapped gas escapes too fast, making the bread dense.

quiz.why: Baking sets the structure, but if the gas escapes too fast, the structure cannot hold it all.

wrong.0: The yeast is killed by the heat, but the gas escape is a physical process happening during the bake.
wrong.1: Gluten is a protein; it does not chemically convert into sugar when heated.
wrong.2: While it shrinks, the primary issue is the rapid loss of internal gas pressure.
